Vignette: Maya, Age 19

Maya is nineteen years old, and she carries herself like someone who is always bracing for something. She sits in the chair with her knees pulled toward her chest, her eyes moving to the door whenever footsteps pass in the hallway outside. She got married six months ago, she says, mostly because she needed someone to feel safe with. She is not sure it is working.

The assault happened fourteen months ago, on a Tuesday evening in early November. Maya had been walking home from a friend's apartment, a route she had taken dozens of times. A man she did not recognize grabbed her from behind in a parking lot two blocks from her building. He beat her and took her phone and her bag. She was on the ground for several minutes before anyone found her. She remembers the cold of the pavement against her cheek and the particular quality of silence that followed — a silence that felt, she says, like the world had simply stopped caring.

In the weeks after, Maya told herself she was fine. She filed a police report, stayed with her mother for a while, and tried to return to the part-time retail job she'd had since high school. The first time a customer came up behind her quickly to reach past her for a product on a shelf, she knocked an entire display over trying to get away from him. She quit that same week. She has not worked since.

Sleep became something that happens to other people. When she does fall asleep, she wakes within an hour or two, heart hammering, convinced someone is in the room. She checks the locks on the apartment door three, sometimes four times before bed, and still she does not feel certain. Her husband, Darian, has started sleeping with a nightlight on because she cannot tolerate the dark, and she feels guilty about this in a way she cannot quite articulate — as though she is slowly making his life smaller to accommodate the wreckage of hers.

During the day, Maya finds it almost impossible to leave the apartment alone. She and Darian live near a large parking lot, and she cannot look at it directly. She takes the long way to the mailbox. She has declined every invitation from friends over the past year and has watched those friendships quietly dissolve. She does not blame anyone for drifting away. She feels, she says, like she is already somewhere else — like she is watching her own life through thick glass, present in body but not in any way that matters.

What frightens her most are the moments when the memory comes back without warning — not as a thought she is having, but as something happening right now. The smell of cold air, the sound of footsteps behind her on pavement, a man's raised voice in a neighboring apartment — any of these can send her back to that parking lot in an instant. Her body responds as though fourteen months have not passed at all. Afterward, she is exhausted and ashamed, and she wonders, not for the first time, whether this is simply who she is now.

She does not talk about the assault with Darian. She is afraid of what it would do to him, she says, and also afraid of what it would do to her — that saying it out loud would make it more real, or that he would look at her differently. She has become skilled at changing the subject, at performing a version of herself that seems functional. Most days, she says, she gets through it. But getting through it and living are not the same thing, and somewhere beneath the careful management of each hour, she knows this. She came in, she says quietly, because she is tired of being nineteen and feeling like her life is already behind her.
